segments.text: Hello again.
Day four.
The sharpest part is usually behind you by now, or close to it.
And sometimes what comes next isn't a craving at all.
It's a flat feeling.
Grey.
A bit bored.
As if someone turned the color down on the day.
If that's you today, I want you to know two things.
It's common.
And it passes.
Here's what's going on.
For a long time, nicotine gave you a small lift, many times a day.
You saw in the prep week what that lift mostly was.
The gap closing.
Relief from a restlessness the last one left behind.
But it was still a lift, and your day was built around dozens of them.
Now they've stopped, and for a little while, the ordinary good things can feel quieter than they are.
A cup of coffee.
A song.
Finishing a job.
There's a thought that likes to show up here.
It says, "See?
You were happier before."
You know that passenger now.
It's describing the dip, not your life.
Studies of people who stopped smoking found that, once withdrawal settled, they were on average less anxious and less stressed than people who kept smoking.
So this isn't a sign that something's missing for good.
It's the stretch in between.
You don't fix a flat day with one big thing.
You nudge it, with small things, often.
Let's do one right now.
Wherever you are, look for the nearest daylight.
A window, a doorway.
If you can, go and stand in it.
If you can't, just turn toward it.
Let your shoulders drop.
And take two slow breaths, the way you practiced in the prep week.
In through your nose, a little extra sip at the top, and a long, slow breath out.
Once more.
Now notice your body.
Not whether you feel good.
Just whether anything shifted, even slightly.
A long, slow breath out helps many people settle.
And that took less than a minute.
That's a lift.
Daylight, a breath, music, cold water on your face, a short walk, a call with someone who makes you laugh.
None of them is dramatic.
They add up.
The trick is to choose them now, while you're listening to me and feeling reasonably steady.
On a flat day, you won't feel like choosing.
You'll just need the list.
In a moment, you'll pick three.
And one more thing, because it matters.
Feeling low for a while after stopping is common.
But if low mood lasts more than about two weeks, or gets in the way of daily life, please talk to your doctor.
And if you ever feel you can't cope or keep yourself safe, get help straight away.
There are numbers for where you live in the app.
Four days.
The color comes back.
I'll see you tomorrow.
